title: Chapter 37: The Stalk of Grass 5
content:
Chapter 37

Lan Jingyi plastered his eye to the slit in the wooden door, only to throw his whole body flat against the planks a second later, completely wide-eyed. "S-so—there's so many!"

"Walking corpses?" Wei Wuxian asked. "How many is 'many'?"

"I don't know!" Jingyi stammered. "The entire street is packed! Hundreds of them, and more are crawling out by the second! Those two paper figures are on their last legs!"

If the paper sentries fell, that endless sea of corpses would come crashing through the door. If the kids fought back with swords, they’d get drenched in corpse-poison powder, and frantic swordplay would only pump the venom straight to their hearts; if they didn't fight back, they'd be torn to shreds. Xiao Xingchen gripped his sword, bracing himself to shove the door open—clearly intending to burn through his dying embers to buy them a few precious seconds—but a sickly violet flush surged across his cheeks, dropping him straight to the floorboards.

Wei Wuxian caught him lightly. "Just sit tight. I'll wrap this up in a second."

Without missing a beat, he dragged his right index finger across the edge of Lan Jingyi's sword, letting the blood bead.

"You're doing the Paper Puppet Invocation again?!" Jingyi balked. "Two dabs per eye—by the time you finish dotting every figure in here, you'll bleed dry! Want me to lend you some?"

Several other disciples immediately began shoving up their sleeves. "I can spare some too..."

Wei Wuxian didn't know whether to laugh or cry. "Keep your blood. Anyone got a blank talisman?"

These juniors were still green; none of them had reached the level where they could draw and activate spells on the fly, meaning their pouches were strictly stocked with pre-drawn charms. Lan Sizhui shook his head. "None, Senior."

"A used one works fine," Wei Wuxian said easily.

Sizhui promptly pulled a stack of yellow talismans from his Qiankun pouch. Wei Wuxian plucked just one from the pile, skimmed it, and pressed his bloody index and middle fingers together, slashing a wild, sweeping stroke from top to bottom over the cinnabar markings. Fresh crimson blended seamlessly with old vermilion, birthing an entirely new sigil. With a crisp flick of his wrist, the yellow paper burst into flames. Wei Wuxian held out his left palm, catching the fluttering black flakes as they drifted down. He curled his fingers around the ash, lowered his head, and gently blew the blackened powder over the rows of waiting paper dolls, murmuring under his breath:

"Wildfire leaves no ash behind;

Spring winds breathe the soul to life."

A cloud of dark soot washed over the paper faces.

At the very front of the line, an underworld warden raised his heavy broadsword from the dirt and hauled it casually onto his broad shoulder.

Beside him, an exquisitely dressed paper beauty with towering dark hair slowly lifted a pale right hand, flexing her long, gossamer fingers with lazy grace—for all the world like a bored aristocrat admiring her freshly lacquered crimson talons. At her hem stood a pair of paper children. The golden boy playfully tugged the jade maiden's braided pigtail; in response, the girl shot out a nine-inch serpent’s tongue, plunging it viciously through the boy's chest like a venomous pike before snapping it back behind her lips. The boy opened his maw wide, baring two rows of razor-sharp white teeth, and clamped down hard on her forearm. The two little dolls were brawling among themselves before the fight had even begun.

Two or three dozen paper figures began swaying and stretching in unison, limbering up like prizefighters before a match, rustling and muttering among themselves in a chorus of papery whispers. They weren't living flesh, but they were more alive than anyone in the room.

"Hold your breath," Wei Wuxian instructed.

He stepped clear of the entrance, giving the room a graceful, theatrical sweep of his hand to clear the runway.

The wooden doors blasted wide. A blast of rancid, sickeningly sweet corpse stench billowed through the opening, sending the boys scrambling to bury their faces into their sleeves. With an ungodly roar, the lead warden charged headlong into the fray, the rest of the paper army pouring out in a ruthless white wave behind him.

The doors slammed shut behind the last paper soldier. Wei Wuxian turned back. "Nobody breathed that in, right?"

A chorus of muffled nos came back from behind their sleeves. Satisfied, Wei Wuxian knelt to help Xiao Xingchen up, scanning the room for somewhere clean to lay him down, but the floor was thick with grime; the man had no choice but to rest on the cold, dusty flagstones. Xiao Xingchen's knuckles remained white around the hilt of Shuanghua. Surfacing from his half-faint with a weak cough, he rasped softly, "That just now... was it the Paper Puppet Invocation?"

"I dabble," Wei Wuxian replied smoothly.

Xiao Xingchen managed a faint, bittersweet smile. "Mm... Against a swarm like that, it really is the most effective art."

A brief pause hung between them before he added, "Even so... walking this path leaves one dreadfully vulnerable to the backlash of the spirits under your command. Even the Yiling Laozu himself, the founder of the craft, could not escape that fate. If I may offer a humble word of advice, friend... take greater care going forward. Unless your back is truly against the wall, rely on it sparingly. It would be better to ground yourself in orthodox cultivation..."

Wei Wuxian sighed quietly to himself. "My thanks for the counsel."

Most renowned cultivators wouldn't hesitate to draw rigid battle lines, loudly declaring someone a heretic beyond redemption. Yet here was his martial uncle—barely clinging to life, coughing up black blood—gently warning a stranger to watch out for spiritual backlash. He was clearly a man whose heart was forged from pure, unyielding kindness. Staring down at the thick bandages swathing the man's eyes and recalling everything Xiao Xingchen had suffered, Wei Wuxian couldn't help but feel a deep, aching pity.

Young disciples were usually far too fascinated by the spectacle of heretical arts to bother scolding it. Except for Jin Ling, whose face was perpetually stormy, the rest of the boys were practically glued to the door seam, commentating on the slaughter outside:

"Sweet heavens... look at that paper maiden's claws! One swipe leaves five trenches in the dirt!"

"Why is that little girl's tongue so long and hard?! Is she supposed to be a hanging ghost?!"

"Look at the muscle on that warden! He just hoisted four walking corpses at once—he's gonna slam them! Look, look! Down they go! Smashed to bits!"

Having finished listening to Xiao Xingchen's gentle sermon, Wei Wuxian retrieved the last untouched bowl of spicy congee from the table. "You're heavily poisoned. I have a bowl of... something here. It might take the edge off, or it might do absolutely nothing, and it tastes downright horrific. Want to give it a shot? If you're eager to die, feel free to pass."

Xiao Xingchen accepted the bowl with both hands. "Of course I want to live. One should always choose life if there's a chance."

He tipped the rim to his lips, took a single swallow, and his face instantly hitched. His lips clamped tight, fighting a desperate, heroic battle not to spray the broth across the floorboards. It took him a long, silent beat to swallow it down before he managed a strained, impeccably polite, "...Thank you."

Wei Wuxian whipped around to face the boys. "You see that? Do you see how a gentleman behaves? You spoiled brats complain about every single bite, but look at him!"

Jin Ling sneered, "Did you even cook it? Aside from dumping a handful of bizarre trash into the pot at the end, what the hell did you actually do?!"

Xiao Xingchen murmured gently, "Though... having given it some thought, if I had to drink this every day, I think I would choose death."

Jin Ling burst into loud, merciless laughter, and even Lan Sizhui couldn't hold back a muffled snort. Wei Wuxian gave them a deadpan look, prompting Sizhui to hastily school his expression back to pristine discipline.

Right then, Lan Jingyi cheered from the door: "They're done! They cleared the lot! We won!"

Xiao Xingchen hastily set his bowl down. "Don't unbar the door just yet. Be on guard—another wave might be—"

"Pick the bowl back up and finish it," Wei Wuxian interrupted, strolling over to the door to peer through the crack.

The street outside was a scene of unearthly carnage. A thin veil of white fog drifted over clouds of dissipating purple dust. The paper figures were leisurely patrolling the cobblestones, stepping on any stray limbs that still showed a twitch of movement, grinding the meat into paste beneath their embroidered slippers.

Beyond that, the street was dead silent. No fresh corpses in sight.

Just as Wei Wuxian’s shoulders began to drop, an impossibly faint rustle stirred directly above his head.

It was a sound so subtle it barely existed—like someone sprinting across the rooftop tiles with unnerving, weightless grace. His boots barely whispered against the slate. With his sharp senses, Wei Wuxian just barely caught the tiny vibration of shifting clay; Xiao Xingchen, possessing the hyper-tuned hearing of the blind, caught it even faster.

"Above!" Xiao Xingchen called out.

"Scatter!" Wei Wuxian roared.

The ceiling caved inward with a concussive crack. Shattered slate, ancient dust, and dried thatch rained down like hail. Fortunately, the disciples had already bolted to the corners, dodging the falling debris. A dark silhouette plummeted straight through the breach.

He wore deep black Daoist robes, standing tall and ramrod straight like a mountain pine. A horsetail whisk was tucked at his back, a longsword gripped in his hand, his sharp features tilted upward with an aura of aloof, solitary pride.

Yet his eyes held no pupils—only a stark, dead expanse of white.

A fierce corpse!

Before the realization could fully settle in their minds, his blade came thrusting forward like lightning.

The strike was aimed straight at Jin Ling, who was standing closest. Jin Ling brought his sword up to parry, but the sheer, monstrous force behind the blow sent a numbing shockwave up his forearm. Had his blade, Suihua, not been a masterwork brimming with spiritual power, the clash would have shattered the steel and cleaved him in two. Unfazed, the corpse spun into a second strike—fluid as flowing water, merciless as a blood debt—aiming clean for Jin Ling's arm.

Xiao Xingchen lunged forward, parrying the lethal slash with Shuanghua, but the surge of corpse poison caught up with him, and his knees gave out, dropping him unmoving to the dirt.

Lan Jingyi gasped in sheer horror, "Is he dead or alive?! I've never seen a corpse—"

A corpse with footwork this agile, wielding a blade this flawless!

The words died on his tongue because the memory hit him: hehadseen this before.

The Ghost General fought just like this!

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed on the dark cultivator. Thoughts racing, he whipped the bamboo flute from his sash and loosed a piercing, shrill shriek of a note that sent the boys clamping their hands over their ears. Hearing the command, the corpse’s frame hitched, his sword arm trembling violently—yet with a vicious snap, he lunged forward anyway!

He couldn't override it. This corpse already had a master!

Wei Wuxian sidestepped the thunderous thrust, pivoting on his heel to spin a completely different melody into the air. Seconds later, the paper figures patrolling outside vaulted onto the eaves and dropped through the roof's gaping hole. Sensing the ambush, the fierce corpse whipped his blade around in twin arcs, cleaving two paper maidens clean in half from crown to hem. His left hand whipped the horsetail whisk free; thousands of silky white strands hardened into steel barbed wire, bursting heads and severing paper limbs with every flick. A single stray brush of those fibers would turn a living man into a bloody sieve.

"Stay back!" Wei Wuxian barked over his shoulder. "Stick to the corners and don't move!"

His fingers danced across the crude bamboo, shifting between manic, mocking trills and soaring bursts of wrath. Despite fighting two-handed with terrifying savagery, the corpse was quickly swarmed as more paper soldiers rained from the ceiling, pressing him from every blind spot. He was holding the line, but running out of room. Out of nowhere, a massive paper warden dropped like an anvil, slamming onto his shoulders and pinning him face-first to the floorboards.

Before he could throw the weight off, three more wardens dropped through the hole, piling on top of him like lead weights.

Underworld wardens were legendary for their brute force; craftsmen packed their frames with heavy materials to give them heft, and once possessed by summoned spirits, they were heavier than lead. A single one hitting you was like catching a falling boulder; taking four in a row without coughing up your internal organs was nothing short of miraculous. Pinned beneath the mountain of paper muscle, the fierce corpse was locked dead to the floor, unable to twitch a finger.

Wei Wuxian walked over, noticing a tear in the fabric over the corpse's back. Smoothing the frayed hemp aside, he found a narrow, clean puncture wound nestled near the left shoulder blade. "Flip him over," he ordered.

The four wardens rolled the corpse onto his back, leaving him staring blankly at the ceiling rafters. Wei Wuxian dragged his bleeding finger across their painted red lips as a reward; the wardens flicked out bright crimson paper tongues, slowly, greedily lapping up the fresh blood like a gourmet treat.

Wei Wuxian looked back down at the corpse. Right over the left breast, near the heart, lay an identical tear—the same clean, narrow puncture. He had been run through the chest with a single thrust of a sword.

The corpse struggled violently under the wardens' grip, a low, guttural snarl rattling in his throat as black blood trickled from the corner of his mouth. Wei Wuxian pinched his jaw, forcing his teeth apart to look inside.

His tongue had been torn out by the roots.

Blind eyes. A severed tongue.

Blind eyes. A severed tongue.

Why did these exact two traits keep turning up together?

Studying the corpse's vacant face, Wei Wuxian was suddenly reminded of Wen Ning's state when he’d been enslaved by those cursed iron nails. Following his gut, he reached down to feel around the corpse's temples.

His fingertips brushed against two tiny metal studs buried in the flesh!

Black skull-piercing nails—designed to dominate high-tier fierce corpses and strip them of their sentience. Not knowing who this man was or whose side he had walked on in life, Wei Wuxian didn't dare yank the pins out blind; he needed answers first. But with his tongue ripped out, the corpse couldn't utter a word even if he woke up.

Wei Wuxian turned to the Lan disciples. "Have any of you studiedInquiry?"

Lan Sizhui raised his hand immediately. "I have. I know the score."

"Did you bring a guqin?"

"I did." Sizhui reached into his Qiankun pouch and pulled out a seven-stringed zither—its woodwork smooth and polished, looking brand new.

Wei Wuxian eyed the instrument. "How's your zither language? Have you used it in the field? Can the spirits you summon tell lies?"

Lan Jingyi piped up, "Hanguang-jun said Sizhui's zither language is passable!"

If Lan Wangji called it "passable," it was definitely rock-solid; the man never exaggerated, and he never gave false praise. Wei Wuxian breathed a little easier.

Sizhui added, "Hanguang-jun taught me to focus on precision rather than breadth. A summoned spirit may refuse to answer, but it cannot speak a lie. If it answers, it will always be the truth."

"Let's get to it, then," Wei Wuxian said.

Sizhui laid the guqin before the corpse's head, smoothing the hem of his robes as he sat cross-legged on the dirt. He tested two strings, nodding once.

"First question," Wei Wuxian instructed. "Ask who he is."

Sizhui centered his breathing, silently running through the incantation before plucking out a measured phrase.

A moment of quiet passed before the strings shivered on their own, ringing out with two sharp, stone-splitting notes.

Sizhui’s eyes went wide.

"What did he say?" Jingyi pressed.

"Song Lan!" Sizhui breathed.

...Song Lan?! Xiao Xingchen’s sworn cultivation partner, Song Zichen?!

Every eye in the room snapped toward the unconscious Xiao Xingchen crumpled on the floor. Sizhui murmured under his breath, "I wonder if he even knows it's Song Lan..."

Jin Ling kept his voice equally hushed. "Probably not. He's blind, Song Lan is mute, and now he's been turned into a brainless killing machine... It's better that he doesn't know."

Wei Wuxian said, "Second question. Ask him who murdered him."

Sizhui carefully plucked out the second phrase.

This time, the silence stretched three times longer than the first.

Just as they were convinced Song Lan's spirit was refusing to answer, the strings trembled, weeping out three heavy, agonizing notes.

"Impossible!" Sizhui blurted out.

Wei Wuxian’s gaze sharpened. "What did he say?"

Sizhui stared at the wood in sheer disbelief. "He said... Xiao Xingchen."

Xiao Xingchen murdered Song Lan?!

Two questions in, and every answer was more devastating than the last. Jin Ling frowned in suspicion. "Did you play the wrong chord?!"

"No," Sizhui protested. "'Who are you?'and'Who killed you?'are the most basic, fundamental phrases inInquiry! They're the very first lines every disciple learns, practiced tens of thousands of times. I double-checked the phrasing—I couldn't have played it wrong."

"Then either your playing was botched, or your translation is garbage!" Jin Ling snapped.

Sizhui shook his head. "If playing it wrong is impossible, mistranslating it is even more so. The characters for 'Xiao Xingchen' are far from common in a spirit's vocabulary. If he had named someone else and I misread it, there's no way it would accidentally spell out this specific name."

Jingyi murmured in a daze, "...Song Lan set out to find the missing Xiao Xingchen, only for Xiao Xingchen to murder him...? Why would he slaughter his dearest friend? He doesn't seem like that kind of person at all!"

"Put that aside for now," Wei Wuxian cut in. "Sizhui, third question: ask who is controlling him."

Sizhui's expression turned grim. Holding his breath, he plucked out the third sequence. Dozens of eyes were pinned to the vibrating strings, waiting for Song Lan's verdict.

Sizhui translated the notes one heavy character at a time:

"The... one... be... hind... you."

The entire room whipped around in unison.

The unconscious Xiao Xingchen was sitting up, resting his chin casually on one propped palm. He offered them a faint, pleasant smile, raised his black-gloved left hand, and snapped his fingers.

The crisp snap struck Song Lan’s ears like an explosion. In a violent blur of motion, the fierce corpse bucked, hurling all four underworld wardens flying across the room!

He vaulted to his feet, wielding both sword and horsetail whisk simultaneously, shearing and whipping the paper wardens into a confetti shower of colorful scraps. The tip of his longsword pressed flush against Wei Wuxian’s throat, while his whisk leveled a lethal threat at the huddled disciples.

In the blink of an eye, the entire room was held hostage.

Jin Ling’s hand dropped to his hilt. Catching the movement out of the corner of his eye, Wei Wuxian barked, "Don't touch that sword! Don't make things worse. Sword for sword, everyone in this room put together isn't a match for this... Song Lan."

In this stolen vessel, his spiritual reserves were laughably weak, and he had no blade of his own. On top of that, they had an unpredictable "Xiao Xingchen" sitting right beside them, motive unknown.

The blind swordsman smiled gently. "The adults need to talk. Why don't you children run along outside?"

He flicked a hand toward Song Lan, who silently obeyed, herding the disciples toward the door with the tip of his blade. Wei Wuxian told the boys, "Step outside for now. You won't be able to help in here anyway. The corpse dust should have settled by now, but don't kick up the dirt, and keep your breathing shallow."

Hearingyou won't be able to helpmade Jin Ling bristle with bitter frustration, but knowing he was truly powerless here, he swallowed his pride and stomped out first. Sizhui hovered at the threshold, clearly torn.

"Sizhui," Wei Wuxian said softly. "You're the most sensible one here. Look after them. Can you do that?"

Sizhui nodded firmly.

"Don't be afraid," Wei Wuxian added.

"I'm not."

"Truly?"

"Truly," Sizhui replied, a faint smile touching his lips. "Senior... you're remarkably like Hanguang-jun."

Wei Wuxian blinked in surprise. "Like him? Where on earth do you see that?" They were night and day!

Sizhui simply smiled without answering and ushered the remaining boys out the door.I don't know how to explain it,the boy thought to himself,but it feels the same. As long as either of those two seniors is standing there, there's simply nothing in this world to be afraid of.

Once the room cleared, "Xiao Xingchen" produced a small crimson pill from his sleeve and popped it into his mouth. "How touching."

The moment the medicine went down, the purplish hue draining his face faded away. Wei Wuxian noted, "An antidote for corpse powder?"

"Indeed," the man replied. "Far more effective than that dreadful slop of yours, wouldn't you say? And sweet, to boot."

Wei Wuxian drawled, "You certainly put on quite the show. Slashing through corpses outside until you were 'exhausted,' taking a sword for Jin Ling, faking a dead faint... was the entire circus just for our benefit?"

The man wagged a finger in the air. "Not for 'their' benefit—strictly for yours. I've long heard of the Yiling Laozu’s legendary renown, and seeing you in the flesh truly exceeds the tales."

Wei Wuxian’s face remained an unreadable mask.

The man smiled. "I take it you haven't told a soul who you really are, have you? That's why I didn't blow your cover. I sent the children away so we could have a private chat behind closed doors. Rather thoughtful of me, wouldn't you say?"

"The walking corpses in Yi City are all under your thumb?" Wei Wuxian asked.

"Naturally. From the moment you walked into this city and blew that whistle, I knew something smelled fishy. So I decided to step onto the stage myself to test the waters. And sure enough—to wield a bottom-tier trick like the Paper Puppet Invocation with that kind of devastating lethality could only be the hand of the creator himself."

They walked the exact same crooked path; one practitioner of the dark arts could never fool another. Wei Wuxian said flatly, "So you've taken a pack of kids hostage. What do you actually want from me?"

The man smiled warmly. "I was hoping Senior could do me a favor. Just a small one."

His mother's martial brother calling him "Senior"—the generational hierarchy was thoroughly scrambled. While Wei Wuxian was privately scoffing, the man produced a Spirit-Trapping Pouch and set it gently onto the table. "Please."

Wei Wuxian laid a hand over the pouch, probing its spiritual contents like a physician checking a pulse. After a moment, he frowned. "Whose soul is this? It's shattered to dust—you couldn't paste this back together with glue. There's barely a dying breath left in here."

The man countered smoothly, "If it were easy to piece together, why on earth would I come begging for your help?"

Wei Wuxian pulled his hand back. "You want me to mend this soul? Forgive my bluntness, but there's barely a trace of spiritual essence left in that bag. Whoever this was suffered horrific torment before passing; they almost certainly took their own life and harbor zero desire to return to this world. If a soul has no will to live, nine times out of ten, they are beyond saving. If I'm not mistaken, whatever scraps are in there were forcibly stitched together by hand; the second they leave that pouch, they'll scatter on the wind. You know this just as well as I do."

The man's smile didn't reach his eyes. "I don't know, and I don't care. You're helping me with this whether you want to or not. Don't forget, Senior—your little flock of disciples is waiting right outside the door, pinning all their hopes on you to lead them out alive."

His voice was a bizarre contradiction: sugary sweet and seemingly affectionate, yet dripping with a senseless, vicious edge. One second he was playfully calling you 'Senior' like an old friend, and the next he wouldn't hesitate to slit your throat.

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Seeing you in the flesh truly exceeds the tales as well. Xue Yang... you're a delinquent through and through, so what's with the Daoist cosplay?"

A brief pause hung in the air.

"Xiao Xingchen" raised a hand and peeled the bandages from his brow.

The linen fell away in loops, revealing a pair of bright, starry eyes glittering in the candlelit gloom.

Completely whole. Undamaged.

It was an undeniably handsome, youthful face, and when he smiled, a pair of sharp little canine teeth peeked out, lending him an almost boyish charm that effortlessly masked the feral brutality lurking behind his gaze.

Xue Yang tossed the bandages aside with a theatrical pout. "Aiya, you caught me."

Wei Wuxian said, "Feigning agony so people's consciences would keep them from checking your eyes; 'accidentally' letting Shuanghua slip from its wrap; 'accidentally' slipping up and calling yourself a wandering Daoist. Not only do you know how to play the victim, you weaponize people's pity, playing the part of a pure, righteous immortal to perfection. If you hadn't displayed far too much knowledge and skill you had no business possessing, I really might have bought that you were Xiao Xingchen."

Besides, duringInquiry, Song Lan's answers to the last two questions had been "Xiao Xingchen" and "the one behind you."

If "the one behind you" was truly Xiao Xingchen, there was zero reason for Song Lan to switch phrasing.

Unless the murderer and the puppeteer were two entirely different people. Song Lan had wanted to warn them that the man was dangerous, but feared naming Xue Yang outright would mean nothing to a bunch of kids, leaving him to point behind them instead.

Xue Yang grinned cheerfully. "Well, he has a sterling reputation and mine is in the gutter! Naturally, wearing his face makes it far easier to win people's trust."

"Masterclass performance," Wei Wuxian applauded dryly.

"Oh, please, you flatter me," Xue Yang brushed it off. "I have a very famous friend who's a true master of the craft; I wouldn't dare hold a candle to him. But enough small talk, Senior Wei—you're doing this favor for me."

Wei Wuxian countered, "The black nails pinning Song Lan and Wen Ning were your handiwork, weren't they? You managed to forge half of the Yin Tiger Tally on your own; why bother asking me to patch up a soul?"

"It's not the same," Xue Yang said. "You're the pioneer. If you hadn't crafted the first half of the Tally, I never could have forged the second. You are far greater than I am. So what I cannot do, you surely can."

Wei Wuxian truly couldn't understand why complete strangers always harbored such boundless, unearned confidence in his abilities. Stroking his chin, he wondered if he should return the flattery. "You're too modest."

"It's not modesty, it's a fact," Xue Yang replied coolly. "I don't make empty boasts. If I say I'm going to wipe out someone's entire clan, I wipe out the entire clan—I don't even leave their dog breathing."

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed. "Like the Yueyang Chang Clan?"

Before Xue Yang could answer, the front doors blasted inward as a dark figure was hurled through the opening!

Wei Wuxian and Xue Yang leaped back from the table in tandem, Xue Yang snatching the Spirit-Trapping Pouch with lightning speed. Song Lan caught the edge of the table with one hand, flipping through the air to absorb the impact before landing lightly on the surface. His head snapped toward the threshold, dark veins pulsing across his cheeks.

Dragging heavy iron chains through a swirl of mist and dark wind, Wen Ning crossed the threshold.

Back when Wei Wuxian played that first shrill note, he had already issued the summons for Wen Ning. He called out to the Ghost General: "Take the fight outside, don't trash the place! Guard the living, and keep the walking corpses away!"

Wen Ning whipped his right arm out, sending a heavy iron chain whistling forward. Song Lan parried with his whisk, the two weapons locking together in a shower of sparks. Wen Ning hauled the chain backward, and refusing to yield his grip, Song Lan was dragged right out into the street.

The disciples, hiding in the doorway of an adjacent shop, craned their necks to watch, completely spellbound. Whisk, chains, and steel collided in an endless, deafening clamor of flying sparks. It was a brawl of terrifying proportions—every strike aimed to maim, every concussive blow bone-deep. Only two fierce corpses could wage a battle this savage; if living men traded blows like this, they’d have been reduced to severed limbs and spilled brains in seconds!

Inside the shop, Xue Yang asked breezily, "Who do you think wins?"

Wei Wuxian didn't look at him. "Is that even a question? Wen Ning takes it."

Xue Yang clicked his tongue. "Such a pity. Even after driving so many skull-piercing nails into his head, he still refuses to obey. Loyal hounds really are a headache."

"Wen Ning isn't a hound," Wei Wuxian said coldly.

Xue Yang threw his head back in laughter. "You do realize how that sounds, don't you?"

Mid-laugh, his blade cleared its sheath, thrusting straight for Wei Wuxian's throat!

Wei Wuxian dodged by a hair's breadth. "Do you always ambush people mid-sentence?"

Xue Yang blinked innocently. "Of course! I'm a delinquent, remember? It's not like you didn't know. Besides, I'm not trying to kill you—just crippling you enough so you'll come quietly and mend this soul for me."

"I told you, I can't do it."

"Don't be so quick to say no! If you don't have a clue on your own, the two of us can brainstorm together." Before he even finished the sentence, another lethal thrust came whistling in.

Wei Wuxian danced through the sea of shredded paper figures, silently noting that the brat’s swordplay was terrifyingly sharp. Seeing Xue Yang's strikes grow faster and deadlier, aiming for his tendons with ruthless precision, Wei Wuxian couldn't help venting: "Taking advantage of the fact that this body's spiritual core is weak, are we?!"

"You bet I am!" Xue Yang beamed.

Having finally crossed paths with someone even more shameless than himself, Wei Wuxian flashed a wicked grin. "Better to cross a gentleman than cross a rogue—they were definitely talking about you. I'm done playing with you. Tagging in a sub!"

Xue Yang chuckled. "A sub? Who, that Hanguang-jun of yours? I sent over three hundred walking corpses to bury him; he—"

Before the boast could clear his lips, a figure draped in pristine white descended from the heavens.

The icy, crystalline blue glare of Bichen cleaved the dark, surging straight for Xue Yang's throat!
